summary: Describes the Router-port Group Management Protocol, developed by Cisco Systems, used between multicast routers and switches so that switches forward multicast traffic only to the routers that might need it. It targets backbone switched networks where several fast routers are interconnected.

plainLanguage.summary: A switch can waste effort sending group messages to every router. RGMP lets routers tell the switch which groups they want, so it only sends where needed.

subtitle: Protocol for routers to tell switches which multicast groups they need

tldr.problem: In switched backbone networks with many routers, multicast traffic floods to all router ports even when most routers don't need it, wasting bandwidth and overloading routers that must discard unwanted traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RGMP lets routers send Hello, Join, and Leave messages to switches on the multicast address 224.0.0.25, telling the switch which groups they want to receive. The switch restricts multicast forwarding to only ports where routers have joined, similar to how IGMP snooping works for host memberships.
tldr.outcome: Deployed in Cisco networks and others. It efficiently restricts multicast in backbone environments but works only when one router connects per switch port.

today: RFC 3488 is an informational document. RGMP was developed by Cisco and deployed in their equipment and in some other vendors' backbone switches. It remains an alternative to IGMP snooping for restricting multicast in backbone networks, though not as widely deployed as IGMP snooping in access networks.

sections.title: The Multicast Flooding Problem
sections.content:
IGMP snooping is a common technique in switches to restrict multicast traffic to ports where hosts have joined groups. However, IGMP snooping has a critical limitation: it cannot restrict traffic to ports connected to routers. Routers do not report their group memberships via IGMP (which hosts use), so the switch has no way to know which groups a router needs. The switch must flood all multicast traffic to all router ports, which wastes bandwidth and forces routers to discard unwanted multicast traffic in software.

In a backbone network where primarily routers connect to backbone switches, this flooding problem is severe. Multiple routers all flooded with the same unnecessary traffic can congest the backbone. The goal of RGMP is to solve this problem in backbone environments: let routers tell switches which groups they actually want to receive.
sections.plainLanguage: Without RGMP, switches send all multicast traffic to every router because they don't know which routers want which groups. Routers end up receiving and throwing away tons of unwanted traffic.

sections.title: How RGMP Works
sections.content:
RGMP uses a simple message format similar to IGMPv2 so that switches with IGMP snooping support can be easily extended with RGMP. All RGMP messages use protocol number 2 (same as IGMP) and are sent with TTL 1 to the multicast address 224.0.0.25, designated by IANA for this purpose.

A router running RGMP on an interface sends four types of messages: Hello (periodic announcement that the router is RGMP enabled), Bye (announcement that RGMP is being disabled on this interface), Join (request to receive a specific multicast group), and Leave (request to stop receiving a group). Each message has a 4-byte format: Type (1 byte), Reserved (1 byte), Checksum (2 bytes), and Group Address (4 bytes).

On the switch side, when a port receives an RGMP Hello, that port becomes RGMP enabled for that router. The switch then listens for Join and Leave messages on that port and establishes forwarding state for groups on a per-group, per-port basis. If an RGMP port stops receiving Hellos (timeout), it reverts to flooding all multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers send messages saying "I am RGMP, please send me group 224.5.5.5, stop sending me group 224.6.6.6." The switch remembers and forwards only what the router asked for.

sections.title: Router and Switch Behavior
sections.content:
On a router: when RGMP is enabled, the router periodically sends Hello messages (default interval 60 seconds) to announce it is RGMP capable. For each group the router's routing protocol wants to receive, it sends periodic Join messages (default 60-second interval). When no longer interested, it sends a Leave message. Routers MUST NOT send Join or Leave for reserved group ranges (224.0.0.x and Cisco-specific groups 224.0.1.39 and 224.0.1.40) so that switches always forward those control groups.

On a switch: when RGMP is enabled, the switch enters a per-port state machine. Upon receiving a Hello on a port, the port becomes RGMP enabled and a timer starts. While the port is RGMP enabled, incoming Join messages trigger forwarding of that group to that port, and Leave messages stop forwarding. The switch always forwards reserved groups (224.0.0.x) to RGMP enabled ports. When the Hello timer expires or a Bye arrives, the port reverts to normal forwarding behavior.

A critical limitation: RGMP supports only one RGMP-enabled router per switch port. Multiple routers on one port will cause traffic blackholing when one router leaves a group that another still wants.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep saying "I am here and I want group A." Switches listen and send traffic only to ports where routers said they want it.

sections.title: Constraints and Interactions
sections.content:
RGMP assumes that routing protocols used (such as PIM-SM) are join-based, where the router explicitly requests multicast groups. This works well with sparse-mode routing but not with dense-mode protocols like DVMRP or PIM Dense-Mode, which expect routers to receive all traffic and prune what they don't need.

For PIM-SM, directly connected sources may not work if the designated router is RGMP enabled, because the DR needs to receive source traffic unconditionally to trigger the registration process. For PIM-SSM or when the DR is not the source's first hop, RGMP works fine.

RGMP does not specify how to handle multicast on inter-switch links (between backbone switches). Multicast will flood on those links if at least one router is connected to each switch. Some implementations support RGMP spoofing, where switches emit RGMP messages on inter-switch links to constrain traffic, but this is not part of the protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: RGMP works best with routing protocols that use explicit joins. If your routing protocol expects to get everything and then prune, RGMP might not help.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Transmitted as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: IGMP-style checksum over the entire RGMP message.

fields.name: Group Address
fields.desc: IPv4 multicast group; zero for Hello and Bye messages.
